blocks.text:
A measuring station tells you how much of something is in the air. It cannot tell you whose it is — from which country, from which sector. No instrument can separate a microgram from a ship from a microgram from a farm, because by the time it arrives they are the same dust.

A model can, and that is the whole addition made here. TNO runs [LOTOS-EUROS](https://airqualitymodeling.tno.nl/lotos-euros/) daily over Europe, and in this version every emission is *labelled* where it leaves the ground — this country, that sector — and the label is carried with the mass through transport, chemistry and deposition. The labels are fractions of the concentration and they are made to add up to one, so every microgram in a cell belongs to somebody. One run answers it for all sources at once; the older way — switch a sector off, run again, take the difference — changes the chemistry while it is at it, and so answers a slightly different question ([Kranenburg et al., 2013](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/6/721/2013/); [TOPAS](https://airqualitymodeling.tno.nl/topas/topas-documentation/)).

The model is a box, and air crosses its edges. What blows in over the boundary — and what was already in the air when the run began — is not worked out here: it is taken from a global model and given a label of its own ([CAMS](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2023-06/LOTOS-EUROS%20Fact%20sheet.pdf)). So one of the shares you can read off is *from outside*, and that one is assumed rather than computed. It has to be: without it the fractions would not add up, and the pollution that genuinely came from elsewhere would be handed to whoever is nearest.

Every figure below is a live node of this flow. Start by choosing what to ask about: these are the pollutants the publisher offers, read from its own config rather than typed here.

blocks.caption: What there is to ask about

blocks.text:
Two networks measure it here, and they could not be more different. The official one, RIVM’s Luchtmeetnet, contributes 93 reference stations — known instruments on known sites, as close to the truth as measuring gets. The citizen network, [Samen Meten](https://www.rivm.nl/lucht/meten-modelleren-berekenen/samen-meten), contributes 3,166 small sensors on balconies and fences.

One sensor is worse than one station at almost everything; three thousand are better than 93 at the one thing a map needs, which is being somewhere. Precision and coverage are different virtues.

The map underneath the stations is the model: a value per cell, about 1.4 by 1.7 km, for the day the publisher last computed. The markers are the network you chose — and only the stations that can answer, because a station without an instrument for this pollutant, or one the model does not label, is a dot you could press for nothing.

blocks.caption: The model underneath, the measurements on top

blocks.text: Press one. That station comes back taken apart twice — by sector and by country, what was done and where it was done. Same bar, same day, cut two ways: one bar per day, its height the total, each band a share of it. `Boundary` is what blew in over the edge of the model; `Seasalt` and `Saharan Dust` are nobody’s to reduce; the rest is a list of decisions somebody could make.

The same model, the same labels, one zoom level out: cells of roughly 22 by 28 km from 30°N to 71°N, and the EEA’s network on top of them. Neither picture is more true than the other — a cell is an average, and an average over 1.4 km is still an average over a motorway, a park and the house you live in.

It is a second map rather than a second layer because a view fitted to both is a view fitted to Europe, in which the Netherlands is forty pixels across.

Add the labels up over the Netherlands and roughly a third of the particulate matter people put there is Dutch; two thirds crossed a border ([Hendriks et al., 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1352231012011673)). Which is what makes the question worth asking at all: the WHO’s guideline for long-term PM2.5 is 5 µg/m³, the EU’s limit falls to 10 in 2030, and the European Environment Agency attributes about 172,000 deaths in 2023 to what is left above it ([EEA, 2025](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/harm-to-human-health-from-air-pollution-burden-of-disease-status-2025)). Knowing that two thirds came from abroad is not an excuse. It is a list of the conversations that have to happen.

This page and that graph are two readings of the same JSON. {{!flow:Show me the flow}}
